t.7.2.1: Having heard those words of the great-souled Rāghava, the greatly radiant Kumbhayoni spoke this speech.
t.7.2.2: Listen, O king, to what happened: whose energy and strength were so great, how he slew his enemies in battle, and how he could not be slain by his foes.
t.7.2.3: O Rāghava, I shall tell you of this lineage and birth of Rāvaṇa, and likewise of the granting of the boons that were given to him.
t.7.2.4: Long ago, in the Kṛta age, O Rāma, there was a mighty brahmarṣi named Pulastya, a son of Prajāpati, who was like the Grandsire himself in person.
t.7.2.6: But he, that bull among sages, for the sake of practising dharma, went to the hermitage of Tṛṇabindu on the slope of Meru, the great mountain, and dwelt there.
t.7.2.5: His virtues, in righteousness and likewise in character, cannot be fully recounted; for one can only say, by his name, that he is the son of Prajāpati.
t.7.2.7: That righteous-souled one practised austerities, his senses restrained through Vedic recitation. But maidens, going to his hermitage, created obstacles for him.
t.7.2.8: The daughters of the gods and of the serpents, and those who were daughters of royal sages, and the Apsarases too, came to that place, sporting there.
t.7.2.9: Because the grove could be enjoyed in every season and because of its loveliness, those maidens would constantly go to that place and play there.
t.7.2.10: Then the great sage, of mighty splendour, grew angry and declared: "Whatever maiden comes within my sight shall conceive a child."
t.7.2.11: But all of them, having heard the words of the great-souled one, went back; frightened by fear of the brahmin's curse, they did not approach that place.
t.7.2.12: But the daughter of the royal sage Tṛṇabindu did not hear that; going to his hermitage, she wandered about quite fearlessly.
t.7.2.13: At that very time, the great sage, son of Prajāpati, his splendour made radiant by austerity, was engaged there in the recitation of the Vedas.
t.7.2.14: But she, having heard the sound of the Veda and having seen that ascetic rich in austerities, became pale of body, with the child within her body plainly manifest.
t.7.2.15: But she, deeply alarmed on seeing that change in her own form, wondered, "What is this that has come upon me?", and went and stood before her father.
t.7.2.16: Seeing her in that condition, Tṛṇabindu then said: "Why do you bear this form, so unbefitting to yourself?"
t.7.2.18: But earlier I went alone to the divine hermitage of the great sage Pulastya, whose self was purified, in search of my own companions.
t.7.2.17: But the distressed maiden, folding her hands in reverence, said to the ascetic: "I do not know, father, the reason by which my form has become like this."
t.7.2.19: And I do not see there any friend of mine who has come; and having seen the change in my form, I have come here.
t.7.2.21: But he, having learned of that curse of the great sage of purified soul, took his daughter, went to Pulastya, and spoke these words.
t.7.2.20: But the royal sage Tṛṇabindu, whose radiance shone forth through his austerity, entered into meditation, and saw that this too had arisen from the act of the sage.
t.7.2.22: O blessed one, great sage, accept this daughter of mine, adorned by her own virtues alone, as an alms offered to you of my own accord.
t.7.2.23: She will always be devoted to serving you, who are engaged in the practice of austerities and whose senses are worn down by discipline; of this there is no doubt.
t.7.2.24: Then, as the righteous royal sage was speaking those words, the twice-born one, wishing to take the maiden, said to him simply, "Very well."
t.7.2.25: Having given her away, the king then went to his own hermitage. The maiden too dwelt there, pleasing her husband with her virtues, and he of great splendour, being pleased, spoke these words.
t.7.2.26: Blessings on you! I am greatly pleased by the wealth of your virtues; therefore today I bestow on you a son equal to myself in virtues, the perpetuator of both our lineages, who will be renowned as Paulastya.
t.7.2.27: Since the Veda was heard by you here while I was reciting it, your son shall therefore be named Viśravas; of this there is no doubt.
t.7.2.28: Thus addressed, that maiden, with a heart full of joy, in a very short time gave birth to a son, Viśravas.
t.7.2.29: He, Viśravā, the foremost of sages, became renowned throughout the three worlds, endowed with purity and righteousness, and, like his father, devoted to austerity.
